subject: AI & Agents
title: AI Hallucinations: Confident and Wrong
description: A short lesson to help you apply AI Hallucinations: Confident and Wrong.

hook.text: A lawyer cites six court cases in a brief. The judge checks. None of them exist. AI invented them.

buildup.text: LLMs generate text that sounds authoritative regardless of whether the content is factually correct.

discovery.text: Hallucinations happen because the model predicts plausible words, not verified facts.

twist.text: The more confidently AI states something, the more people trust it — even when it's completely fabricated.

climax.text: Retrieval-augmented generation helps ground answers in real sources, but hallucinations persist.

punchline.text: It speaks with certainty. That's the most dangerous part.

quiz.question: Why do AI hallucinations occur in language models?
options: Models predict plausible-sounding words rather than verified facts
AI deliberately lies to confuse users
Hallucinations only happen with outdated models

details.summary: AI hallucinations occur when models generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information with complete confidence. This is an inherent feature of how language models work, not a fixable bug.
details.whyItMatters: Users who trust AI outputs without verification risk spreading misinformation. Understanding hallucinations as a fundamental limitation promotes healthy skepticism toward AI-generated content.
takeaways: LLMs confidently generate false information called hallucinations
Hallucinations arise from how language models predict text
Always verify AI claims against authoritative sources

faq.question: Why do AI models hallucinate false information?
faq.answer: Language models predict statistically likely text sequences. They have no mechanism for verifying factual accuracy. Plausible-sounding false statements can be just as statistically likely as true ones.

faq.question: Can AI hallucinations be prevented?
faq.answer: They can be reduced through retrieval-augmented generation, fact-checking layers, and improved training. But completely eliminating hallucinations is likely impossible with current language model architectures.
